claims.text: Degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 during elevated-temperature oxidizing or reducing exposure is governed mainly by the nature and stability of its surface oxide layer.
Synergistic interactions among Al, Ti, and Cr control formation of mixed oxide films in this alloy.
Increasing Al favors formation of a dense, protective alumina or mixed Al/Cr oxide layer.
Ti and Cr adjust the nucleation and growth kinetics of the surface oxide.
Compositional adjustment can shift the alloy between protective and non-protective oxide formation.
The nominal alloy is an additively manufactured, single-phase FCC alloy with homogeneous elemental distribution.
The nominal alloy has high strength and fatigue performance.
Systematic variation of Al, Ti, and Cr using a NICE-inspired mapping approach can decouple their individual contributions to surface oxide formation.
Preferential oxidation of Al produces the surface oxide, with Ti and Cr modifying its composition, morphology, and stability.
A continuous, dense oxide film minimizes further oxidation and degradation, whereas a porous film is non-protective.
An optimized balance of Al, Ti, and Cr promotes a protective film in oxidizing environments.
Instability or partial reduction of the oxide in reducing environments may accelerate degradation.
Variants with increased Al or an optimized Al/Ti/Cr ratio will form a more uniform, dense, and protective oxide under oxidizing conditions.
The more protective oxide predicted for Al-enriched or optimized variants will produce lower weight gain and less mechanical degradation than the baseline alloy.
Reduced Al or excessive Ti will produce more porous, less protective oxides and accelerate degradation.
Comparable composition-dependent trends will occur in reducing atmospheres, with oxide-reduction dynamics affecting surface integrity.
The baseline Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy undergoes moderate degradation through formation of a mixed oxide film at high temperature.
The proposed mechanism is applicable from approximately 800°C to 1200°C in controlled oxidizing or reducing atmospheres.
The mechanism assumes that the FCC matrix remains stable and that composition changes do not induce phase separation.
The role of Al in forming protective oxides is well documented, whereas the quantitative effects of Ti and Cr on oxide structure and stability remain uncertain.
